questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Covid job losses and whether Denmark's model can help
How to find a well-paid job working from home
Why Microsoft is hiring thousands of new workers
How Denmark became such a rich and happy country
questions.why: They assess the post-Covid job landscape and ask whether Denmark might hold the answer.

questions.q: What downside of working from home do Neil and Sam mention?
options: Their internet connection at home is far too slow
They have to work much longer hours than before
They can't meet friends, share ideas or go for lunch
Their homes are too noisy because of the neighbours
questions.why: Neil mentions not meeting friends or sharing ideas, and Sam adds going out for lunch.

questions.q: Who has found the pandemic especially stressful, according to Sam?
options: Company bosses
People working from home
Students finishing school
Daily workers with no savings
questions.why: Sam says it's been especially stressful for daily workers without savings to pay rent and feed families.

questions.q: What does Elisabeth Reynolds think about recovery in the short term?
options: It has already begun in most parts of the world
It's too early to talk about, as effects will continue
It will be fastest in the US because of its size
It depends only on how quickly a vaccine is found
questions.why: She says we're not yet in a place to talk about recovery and will see the ripple effect for months.

questions.q: What does Elisabeth Reynolds say about current government job support?
options: It can't last long term, so bigger change is needed
It is working well and should stay exactly the same
It is far too small to really help anyone at all
It only helps large companies, not small businesses
questions.why: Sam says she thinks many measures are not sustainable in the long term and more radical change is needed.

questions.q: What must unemployed Danes do in return for generous payments?
options: Pay much higher taxes once they find work again
Move to another city where there are more jobs
Work for the government for a whole year without pay
Accept any job or training the government thinks useful
questions.why: Sam says citizens are expected to commit to any job or training the government thinks is beneficial.

questions.q: According to Jacob Kirkegaard, what is it like for employers in Denmark?
options: They must offer jobs for life
Firing workers is very expensive
It's easy and free to hire and fire people
They pay for all workers' training
questions.why: He says it's very easy to hire and fire people and it doesn't cost you anything.

questions.q: Why do Danish workers feel secure even without a job for life?
options: Their strong trade unions will always protect them
They can retrain with state help and find new work
Most of them own their homes, so they have no rent
They can easily move abroad to work in other countries
questions.why: Kirkegaard says people know they can find another job, with reskilling paid partly by lavish subsidies.
